title: I am: the self's first words
hook: before anything else exists, the self says its first words, then feels its first fear, then its first loneliness
carry: i am, before the ego adds a name
tomorrow: the self split in two — husband and wife, the whole world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gods auditioned every sense, and only prana, the plain breath, couldn't be pierced. Your line was breath is untouched by evil.

A knock on a door. Someone inside calls: who is it? And the answer often comes before any name: it's me. A small habit, easy to miss. The Brihadaranyaka stops to explain it, in the middle of telling how the world began. That habit, it says, goes all the way back to the first moment there was anyone at all: the first words ever spoken, and the two feelings that came right after them.
screen: `WHO IS IT?` → `IT'S ME.` → `THE FIRST WORDS EVER SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: In the beginning, the text says, there was only the self, in the shape of a person. It looked around and saw nothing but itself. And the first thing it said was aham asmi. I am. So it came to be called I. That's why, the text adds, when anyone is called even now, they first say it's me, and then whatever other name they have. Then the self was afraid. That's why, the text says, a person alone is afraid. Then it thought: there's nothing here but me. What am I afraid of? And the fear left. Because, the text says, fear only comes from a second. Then the self had no joy. That's why a person alone has no joy. And it wanted a second. Three moods in a few lines: I am, then fear, then longing. Notice which one thinking can cure. Fear goes the moment the self sees there's nothing else to fear. Loneliness doesn't go that way. It turns into wanting, and the wanting, tomorrow, becomes a whole world. Later Hindu philosophy uses this little word, aham, in two very different ways. Ahamkara, the I-maker, is the ego that says me, mine, my name. And in Advaita Vedanta, the phrase aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from a few lines later in this same chapter, points at an I with no name tacked on after it. The first words in this story come before either one: just I am, and only then the names the ego collects.
screen: `AHAM ASMI: I AM.` · `FEAR COMES FROM A SECOND.` · `ALONE, IT HAD NO JOY.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · then, large: `I AM, BEFORE ANY NAME.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, and notice the plain sense that you're here: not your name, not your job, not whose child or parent you are. Just: I am. If a worry comes, ask it gently, as the self did in the story, what in this room, right now, there is to be afraid of, and then come back to I am.
Aham asmi. I am. In the Brihadaranyaka, the first words the self ever spoke, before there was anything else to speak to.
Your line: i am, before the ego adds a name. Tomorrow, the lonely self finds a way to have a second. Day three hundred sixty-three, done.

howItsDone: Students of the Upanishads read this passage as part of the Brihadaranyaka's creation account; in Vedanta teaching it is often paired with aham brahma asmi, I am Brahman, from the same chapter (1.4.10), one of the great sayings.
